newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lebed hints Moscow would accept NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Lebed hints Moscow would accept NATO expansion.

text.p: Russian security supremo Alexander Lebed voiced grudging acceptance of NATO's plans to expand eastwards on Monday, urging caution on the alliance but saying Moscow would not fly into a panic if it went ahead.

Lebed, a reserve general and strong candidate to succeed Boris Yeltsin if he fails to return to his duties after heart surgery, appealed to his former foes to delay a decision for a generation to allow the bitterness of the Cold War to fade.
"We are all products, victims of the Cold War, we are not going to solve these problems in 24 hours," Lebed told a news conference after a day of meetings with NATO leaders.
But, in comments that contrasted with previous bitter attacks on the expansion plans, he added:
"It is NATO's business what NATO decides. Whatever NATO decides, Russia is not going to go into hysterics."

Russia has tried to link enlargement with a new treaty or charter governing all relations between the two former Cold War foes. It sees expansion as a threat to its security. NATO rejects any idea of linkage.
Lebed said he accepted NATO's right to expand if it wished, going further than any senior Russian figure to date, but said the problem was one of timing.

"The main thing is not to hurry, or you may trip up," Lebed said. NATO intends next year to invite countries to open entry talks with Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic the most likely candidates.

Senior NATO diplomats were divided in their first assessment of the Kremlin newcomer, with some arguing his was simply a change of style rather than substance. Others said it was the clearest signal yet Moscow considered enlargement inevitable.
"He above all insisted on the question of timing as if the principle was now non-negotiable," said one ambassador.
Lebed, a man burning with presidential ambitions, clearly enjoyed his day at the heart of the organisation that for two decades was the enemy "Lion's Den" and in the spotlight of the world's media.
From the moment he arrived in Brussels on Sunday on the invitation of NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana for his first ever trip to the West, Lebed has sought to assume the mantle of a statesman.
His voice is booming, at home on a parade ground, but his comments have been measured; those of a man coming to terms with political skills.
One NATO envoy said he started his address to ambassadors by asking them not to judge him by media reports.
Lebed is prone to colourful language, describing NATO on one occasion as behaving like a drunken hooligan in a kindergarten over its expansion plans.
A senior diplomat described Lebed as a highly intelligent man in a rational "listening mode". There was, he said, no "over-the-top language".
"We are enormously encouraged...We see him as a very important figure whatever the future holds," the official said.
Western officials were clearly eager to gain a first-hand impression of the man who performed so strongly in elections this year.

Lebed is an unknown quantity to the West, familiar largely through his extraordinary voice. For many officials here and in NATO capitals he has the same "maverick" aura as Boris Yeltsin had in the years before he edged Mikhail Gorbachev from power.
He repeated previous warnings that hasty eastward expansion could imperil conventional forces and nuclear arms agreements already signed but not yet ratified by Russia's parliament.
On Tuesday he is scheduled to visit NATO's military command headquarters in the town of Mons, centre of operations for alliance forces in Bosnia.
